The legal precedents mentioned in the text are Smith v. Maryland and Jones v. United States. Smith v. Maryland established the third-party doctrine, which holds that individuals do not have a reasonable expectation of privacy for information voluntarily given to third parties. Jones v. United States applied this principle, referencing Smith v. Maryland to uphold the same idea. The similarity to the case at hand (assuming the case at hand involves third-party data privacy) is that both precedents support the legal argument that voluntarily shared information with third parties is not protected by the Fourth Amendment's reasonable expectation of privacy standard.
